name: Ship of the Flying Dutchman
powers: Doomed to sail the Cape of Good Hope forever; sighting it is an omen.
description: The ghost ship of the Flying Dutchman is a spectral East Indiaman of Dutch maritime legend, doomed to sail the waters off the Cape of Good Hope for ever after its captain, variously named Van der Decken, Falkenberg or the Vanderdecken, swore a blasphemous oath in the teeth of a storm. Mariners reported seeing the phantom vessel from the seventeenth century onward, often glowing with a supernatural light, and a sighting was taken as a warning of disaster or death at sea. The legend was spread by travellers' and sailors' tales in the 1830s, and Richard Wagner's opera Der fliegende Holländer of 1843 fixed the story of the captain condemned to sail until redeemed by a woman's love. No physical vessel survives or ever existed, and the tale is classed as maritime folklore rather than history. The ship has been retold in poems, novels and films, making the Flying Dutchman the archetype of the haunted ship.
source: Maritime legend, from the seventeenth century

name: Tarnhelm
description: Tarnhelm, the magic cap of invisibility in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied, is taken by the hero Siegfried from the dwarf Alberich after he overpowers the dwarf and seizes the Nibelung hoard. Whoever wore the cap, the Tarnkappe, became invisible and could perform feats of strength as though unseen, and Siegfried uses it in the poem to fight in disguise. Richard Wagner transformed the object for his Ring cycle: in Das Rheingold the Tarnhelm is forged by Mime, gives its wearer the power to change shape or travel at speed, and is won by the god Wotan as part of the cursed treasure. The medieval poem's humble cloak thus became, in Wagner's hands, a helmet that enables the deceit and greed at the heart of the Ring. The name, from the German tarnen, 'to conceal', is the classic German equivalent of the cloak of invisibility found across European fairy tales.

name: Frau Holle's Feather Bed
powers: Shaken by Frau Holle, its feathers fall to earth as snow.
description: Frau Holle's feather bed is the great bedding that the old woman shakes out in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Frau Holle' (KHM 24), causing its feathers to fall to earth as snow. The industrious heroine, after her fall into the well and a period of service shaking the bed each morning, is rewarded with a shower of gold, while the lazy sister earns only pitch. The tale explains the seasons through household labour, the winter snow being nothing more than Frau Holle's feathers flying. Frau Holle herself, a fair, long-toothed old woman who rewards diligence and punishes idleness, is sometimes identified by scholars with the Germanic goddess Holda of folklore, who was said to shake her feather pillows to make snow. The episode is among the most famous comic explanations in the Grimms' collection. The feather bed is the story's hinge, turning domestic work into the natural world's weather.

name: Pied Piper's Pipe
powers: Its music charmed rats, and later children, following the piper out of Hamelin.
description: The pipe of the Pied Piper of Hamelin is the magic instrument that, according to the legend, lured the rats of the town of Hamelin to drown in the river Weser in 1284, and then, when the citizens refused to pay the promised reward, drew away a hundred and thirty of their children into a mountainside, never to return. No actual pipe survives, and the whole episode belongs to the semi-legendary medieval tradition of the town and its later retellings, including the Grimms' version and Robert Browning's poem. The date 26 June 1284 is recorded in the town's medieval chronicles, and a window in the church of Hamelin once showed the scene. Scholars have offered many theories for the children's disappearance, from emigration to a children's crusade, but the piper himself remains a figure of folklore. The pipe, whose music charms both beasts and children, has become the archetype of the irresistibly alluring tune.
source: Hamelin tradition; Grimm and Browning retellings

name: The Magic Mirror
powers: Told its owner who was the fairest in the land.
description: The magic mirror of the queen in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Snow White' (KHM 53) is a speaking mirror that answers truly when its owner asks who is the fairest in the land. Each time the queen consults it, the mirror replies that she is fairest of all, until the day it names Snow White, and from that answer springs the queen's jealous persecution of the girl. The mirror thus acts as the story's engine and moral judge, an impartial voice that exposes the truth the queen cannot bear. In the Grimms' version the queen meets her end at Snow White's wedding feast, where she is forced to dance in red-hot shoes, and the mirror's last answer seals her fate. Mirrors that speak and tell the truth appear in folklore across Europe, and the motif was spread worldwide by the 1937 animated film, with its famous lines 'Magic mirror on the wall, who is the fairest of them all?'. The mirror exists only in fiction, but it has become one of the most recognisable objects in fairy tale.

name: Cinderella's Glass Slipper
powers: Fitted only Cinderella, letting the prince find her after the ball.
description: The glass slipper of Cinderella is the shoe lost as the heroine flees the prince's ball, the object that lets the prince find his bride because it fits no other foot in the kingdom. In the Grimms' version, Aschenputtel, the lost shoes are of gold, and the slipper motif belongs to the older tale-type in which the hero proves identity by an object that fits only the true owner. It was Charles Perrault's 1697 version, with its shoe of glass, that fixed the slipper in popular imagination, and the fragility of glass made it a perfect emblem of the tale's magic and brevity. Folklorists note that shoe-matching scenes occur in versions of the tale from China, where the heroine loses a shoe, to Europe, making it one of the oldest plot devices in storytelling. The glass slipper appears in no surviving material object, and no such slipper exists. It remains, with the pumpkin coach, the defining image of the Cinderella story.
source: Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen no. 21; Perrault

name: The Six Swans' Shirts
powers: Thrown over her swan brothers, restored them to human form.
description: The six shirts of the Grimms' fairy tale 'The Six Swans' (KHM 49) are woven by the princess from stinging nettles to break the enchantment that has turned her six brothers into swans. For years she must gather the nettles, spin and sew the shirts in complete silence, and her vow costs her dearly when her children are taken from her and she is condemned rather than speak. When the shirts are at last finished and thrown over the swans, her brothers become men again, though the youngest is left with a wing instead of an arm because one shirt was not finished. The tale belongs to the family of swan-brother stories, and the same task of weaving nettle shirts appears in Hans Christian Andersen's 'The Wild Swans'. The shirts are the tale's central ordeal, testing the sister's endurance, silence and faith. The story was told throughout Germany and is preserved in the Grimms' collection.

name: Briar Rose's Spinning Wheel
powers: Pricked the princess and cast the whole castle into a hundred-year sleep.
description: The spinning wheel in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Briar Rose' (Dornröschen, KHM 50) is the instrument of the sleeping curse: the princess pricks her finger on its spindle, and the whole castle falls asleep for a hundred years. The king had ordered every spindle in the land burned to cheat the witch's prophecy, but an old woman in a forgotten tower still spins, and curiosity leads the princess to the fatal prick. When the prince at last cuts through the hedge of thorns and wakes the princess with a kiss, the spindle's curse is undone and the castle stirs back to life. The tale is the German form of the widespread Sleeping Beauty story, and the spinning wheel is its local signature, replacing the flax and distaff of older versions. Spinning in folklore is linked with fate, age and magic, so the wheel carries symbolic weight beyond the plot. The story was popularised in the Grimms' collection and in Perrault's and later cinematic retellings.

name: The Golden Goose
powers: Stuck fast anyone who touched it, drawing a growing chain of followers.
description: Die goldene Gans, the golden goose of the Grimms' fairy tale of the same name (KHM 64), is found by the simpleton Dummling in the wood after he shares his food with a little grey man. The goose is made of gold, and it sticks fast to anyone who touches it, so that when the simpleton carries it home the innkeeper's daughters, the parson and the sexton all become stuck to it in a growing chain. The absurd procession makes the sad princess laugh for the first time in years, and by the tale's rules this wins Dummling her hand and half the kingdom. The goose is the classic fairy-tale marvel: absurd, adhesive and socially levelling, rewarding the kind-hearted simpleton over his clever brothers. The Grimms recorded the tale from German oral tradition in the early nineteenth century. The goose exists only in fiction, but its picture of a laughing kingdom remains one of the most cheerful images in the collection.
